content:
As far as I can find there is no DecidableEq instance for Std.HashMap in the lean4 standard library. Is there a reason why there cant be or is it just not implemented yet?

I can see that Mathlib has a DecidableEq Finmap, but for my application I would like the performance of an actual hash map.
docs#Std.HashMap does not have well-behaved equality, use docs#Std.ExtHashMap instead.
Or, if you're fine with just being able to compare maps, you can also use a == b on regular hash maps.

So after some more searching, I found this comment in lean4

In contrast to regular hash maps, Std.ExtHashMap offers several extensionality lemmas
and therefore has more lemmas about equality of hash maps. This however also makes it lose the
ability to iterate freely over hash maps.

Why does ExtHashMap loose the ability to iterate over its elements? I do not follow this logic.

My application needs both DecidableEq and iteration so I seem to be stuck.

Depending on in which order you insert elements into the hash map, the order of iteration can differ even though the resulting maps are equivalent in the sense that they contain the same key-value pairs. So one has to choose one of these:

  • Have two hash maps be equal iff they contain the same key-value pairs, but then there's no well-defined iteration because the order is not well-defined
  • Have iteration. But then many lemmas we have for the extensional hash map are simply wrong because the LHS and RHS have different iteration order.

May I ask what your application is? Perhaps we can #xy it or find another solution.

The problem is that equal maps must produce equal results for every function; however, iteration might be order-dependent. In the future we might get iteration operations that require a proof that the operation is not order-dependent but we don't have that yet. Again, if you don't need mathematical equality and you're just fine with being able to compare hash maps, a == b should work just fine. Alternatively, you can use Std.ExtTreeMap which doesn't have this problem because all values are already sorted.
Depending on your application, you could consider using an ExtTreeMap, which is a map ordered by its keys. If the order is sufficiently strict (TransOrd), you can iterate over it.

Ahh, I see. This makes sense. I'll give ExtTreeMap a try, but I'd prefer the performance characteristics of a hash map. Maybe there could be some ExtHashMap.toListSorted function that takes a comparison operator on keys and returns a list of (key,value) pairs sorted by key (not sure how that would work for the dependent maps though).

I'm working on formalising memory concurrency models (porting archsem to lean). The systems memory I'd like to model as a hash map indexed by address where empty means undefined.

In our collection of lean projects, we implemented many useful functions and lemmas for hash maps and sets. Function ExtDHashMap.fold can be used for iterating over ext hash map (link). We also have computable functions for producing the list of sorted elements: ExtDHashMap.toList and DHashMap.toSortedList (both require LinearOrder on keys). We share this in case it's of interest.
